questions.stem: An antibody-coated tumor cell is recognized by the CD16 Fc receptor on the effector cell shown; Fc cross-linking triggers degranulation and the target dies by apoptosis. What is this killing mechanism called?

explanation.summary: NK cells express CD16 (FcγRIII), which binds the Fc region of IgG coating a target cell. Cross-linking triggers release of cytotoxic granules, killing the antibody-coated cell by ADCC. This differs from complement lysis and from phagocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: NK cells express CD16 (FcγRIII), which binds the Fc region of IgG coating a target cell. Cross-linking triggers release of cytotoxic granules, killing the antibody-coated cell by ADCC. This differs from complement lysis and from phagocytosis.

questions.stem: The cell on the right kills its target using granules containing perforin and granzymes (as well as Fas-FasL). A patient with a mutation causing nonfunctional perforin would have MOST impaired ability to:

choices.label: B
choices.text: Degranulate mast cells in allergic responses

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kill virus-infected and tumor cells via CD8+ T cells and NK cells

explanation.summary: Perforin lets granzymes enter target cells to trigger apoptosis, the core cytotoxic mechanism of CD8+ CTLs and NK cells. Loss-of-function causes impaired cytotoxicity (e.g., familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis).
explanation.whyCorrect: Perforin lets granzymes enter target cells to trigger apoptosis, the core cytotoxic mechanism of CD8+ CTLs and NK cells. Loss-of-function causes impaired cytotoxicity (e.g., familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis).

questions.stem: A transplant patient on chronic prednisone develops thin skin that bruises easily and pink-purple abdominal striae. These skin changes result from glucocorticoid inhibition of what?

explanation.summary: Glucocorticoids suppress fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis, thinning the dermis. The weakened dermal connective tissue tears to reveal underlying vessels, producing wide pink-purple striae and easy bruising characteristic of Cushingoid skin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glucocorticoids suppress fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis, thinning the dermis. The weakened dermal connective tissue tears to reveal underlying vessels, producing wide pink-purple striae and easy bruising characteristic of Cushingoid skin.

questions.stem: This figure depicts a rejection developing over days to weeks, featuring recipient CD8+ T cells attacking graft parenchymal cells and endothelium (endothelialitis). Compared with hyperacute rejection, what is the principal mechanism of this (acute) rejection?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrosis and vascular narrowing developing over years

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preformed recipient antibodies present before transplant

explanation.summary: Acute rejection occurs days to weeks after transplantation and is driven chiefly by recipient T cells (notably CD8+ cytotoxic T cells) recognizing donor HLA, with a variable antibody-mediated component (endothelialitis). It is distinct from antibody-driven hyperacute rejection (minutes-hours) and chronic rejection (months-years).
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute rejection occurs days to weeks after transplantation and is driven chiefly by recipient T cells (notably CD8+ cytotoxic T cells) recognizing donor HLA, with a variable antibody-mediated component (endothelialitis). It is distinct from antibody-driven hyperacute rejection (minutes-hours) and chronic rejection (months-years).

questions.stem: This process, developing over months to years after solid-organ transplantation, is illustrated. What is the characteristic vascular lesion responsible for graft failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Granulomatous destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutrophilic fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls within minutes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Massive interstitial hemorrhage from platelet thrombi

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complement-mediated lysis of graft endothelium by preformed antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Concentric intimal smooth-muscle proliferation causing vessel occlusion (graft arteriosclerosis)

explanation.summary: Chronic rejection is driven by recipient CD4+ T cells and macrophages responding to graft alloantigens, secreting cytokines that stimulate intimal smooth-muscle proliferation and fibrosis, progressively occluding vessels over months to years. Hyperacute rejection (preformed antibodies) occurs in minutes and acute rejection over days to weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic rejection is driven by recipient CD4+ T cells and macrophages responding to graft alloantigens, secreting cytokines that stimulate intimal smooth-muscle proliferation and fibrosis, progressively occluding vessels over months to years. Hyperacute rejection (preformed antibodies) occurs in minutes and acute rejection over days to weeks.

questions.stem: A naive strain B mouse rejects a strain A skin graft in 14 days; a second strain A graft placed later is rejected in only 6 days. What accounts for the accelerated second-set rejection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Innate complement activation triggered by the second graft

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of MHC expression on the second graft

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immunologic memory (memory T cells generated by the first graft)

explanation.summary: Second-set rejection is faster and more vigorous because the first exposure generated antigen-specific memory T lymphocytes against strain A alloantigens. Specificity and memory are defining features of the adaptive immune response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Second-set rejection is faster and more vigorous because the first exposure generated antigen-specific memory T lymphocytes against strain A alloantigens. Specificity and memory are defining features of the adaptive immune response.

questions.stem: This graph of infant serum immunoglobulins shows a transient dip in IgG at roughly 3-6 months of age. What causes this physiologic nadir?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A Bruton tyrosine kinase mutation blocking all B-cell development

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of maternal IgA from breast milk

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal transplacental IgG has been catabolized before the infant's own IgG production is fully established

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thymic aplasia (DiGeorge syndrome) preventing T-cell help

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autoantibody-mediated destruction of infant plasma cells

explanation.summary: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects the newborn, then declines over the first months of life. Because the infant's own IgG synthesis ramps up more slowly, a transient physiologic hypogammaglobulinemia appears around 3-6 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects the newborn, then declines over the first months of life. Because the infant's own IgG synthesis ramps up more slowly, a transient physiologic hypogammaglobulinemia appears around 3-6 months.

questions.stem: In the postnatal gut mucosa shown, the lumen is defended by secretory antibody even before the infant's own mucosal immunity matures. What is the major source of this early protective secretory IgA?

explanation.summary: Secretory IgA in breast milk and colostrum coats the neonatal gut mucosa, providing passive mucosal immunity. M cells overlying Peyer's patches sample luminal antigen, but the infant's own robust secretory IgA production develops only over the first months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secretory IgA in breast milk and colostrum coats the neonatal gut mucosa, providing passive mucosal immunity. M cells overlying Peyer's patches sample luminal antigen, but the infant's own robust secretory IgA production develops only over the first months.

questions.stem: This graph tracks the site of hematopoiesis across gestation. Which organ is the predominant site of blood-cell production during the middle of fetal development (around months 4-6)?

explanation.summary: Hematopoiesis begins in the yolk sac, shifts to the fetal liver (with a brief splenic contribution) in mid-gestation, then moves to the bone marrow, which becomes the definitive site by birth and remains so in adults.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hematopoiesis begins in the yolk sac, shifts to the fetal liver (with a brief splenic contribution) in mid-gestation, then moves to the bone marrow, which becomes the definitive site by birth and remains so in adults.

questions.stem: This schematic traces the origin of long-lived tissue-resident macrophages (such as microglia, alveolar, and skin macrophages). What is their principal embryonic source?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yolk-sac and fetal-liver progenitors, seeded before birth and self-renewing in tissue

explanation.summary: Many tissue-resident macrophages arise from yolk-sac and fetal-liver progenitors during embryogenesis and maintain themselves by local self-renewal, largely independent of adult bone-marrow-derived monocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many tissue-resident macrophages arise from yolk-sac and fetal-liver progenitors during embryogenesis and maintain themselves by local self-renewal, largely independent of adult bone-marrow-derived monocytes.

questions.stem: The balance of signals shown determines whether an NK cell kills its target. Loss of which surface molecule on a virally infected or tumor cell most strongly tips the balance toward NK-mediated killing?

choices.label: D
choices.text: MHC class I (removing the inhibitory signal)

explanation.summary: NK cells integrate inhibitory signals delivered by MHC I with activating signals from stress-induced ligands. Downregulation of MHC I ('missing self'), together with activating-ligand engagement and cytokines such as IFN, promotes lytic granule release.
explanation.whyCorrect: NK cells integrate inhibitory signals delivered by MHC I with activating signals from stress-induced ligands. Downregulation of MHC I ('missing self'), together with activating-ligand engagement and cytokines such as IFN, promotes lytic granule release.
